title: AFL finals: where the Sydney v Fremantle preliminary final will be won and lost - The Guardian
content: The Swans are within touching distance of an unlikely grand final spot while the Dockers have their campaign for a first premiership back on track Sydney’s season was meant to be dead and buried by now. The club-imposed suspension of five players for breaching club standards was thought to have weakened the side to such an extent that a straight-sets finals exit was all but guaranteed. But while the spotlight was on the absent players, a galvanised group of those who remained – one still sprinkled with stardust – dialled up the heat to stun Brisbane and surge into a home preliminary final. The emotion-charged triumph made the Swans the 13th team to win a qualifying final by more than 50 points since 2000. Eleven of the previous 12 teams then earned a spot in the decider. But for all of their newfound momentum, Dean Cox’s side have to overcome the loss of another pivotal player after captain Callum Mills sustained a serious knee injury against the Lions. The Swans have turned doubters into believers with the way their players have stepped up in the face of adversity. But it would be another chapter in a story for the ages if they can beat the minor premiers to reach a third grand final in five seasons. Fremantle are taking a longer route than hoped towards the club’s second men’s decider with an away preliminary final. But the Dockers showed they have a steel to them as they fought off a serious challenge from the battle-hardened Cats to bounce back in a high calibre semi-final. Justin Longmuir’s side can take confidence from a decent record at the SCG with two wins in their past three games at the venue while going down by under two goals in their most recent visit last year. The minor premiers can also turn to slamming on 100 points in a half when they overran the Swans in round 18 to claim a statement win in the top-of-the-ladder clash. Sydney are without their skipper on Friday, three of their biggest stars and a couple of role players for the rest of the season. But they still have the forward firepower that was enough to blow away the back-to-back premiers. The Swans had the leading attack for points scored through the home-and-away campaign and loaded up with another 141 points – their highest score ever in a final – as they crushed the Lions. They only needed six goalscorers to pile on 21 majors as Logan McDonald (six), Charlie Curnow (five), Tom Papley (five) and Hayden McLean (three) all enjoyed a day out in a warning to the Dockers of the spread of weapons they need to contain. The Swans have become renowned for their run-and-gun gameplan. But they have quietly been building a brand for the added intensity of finals as the top side for scores from clearance with a 14-0 record when they outscore the opposition from the source. Cox’s side dominated scoring from stoppage in their qualifying final as they restricted the Lions to their equal season-low of one goal from the source, while exploding out of the middle themselves for 39 points from centre clearances. Fremantle showed they can be just as damaging at scoring from centre clearance as they booted 45 points from the source in their semi-final against Geelong. Shai Bolton was the early beneficiary as the Dockers twice stormed out of the middle for the livewire to boot the opening two goals of the game. But there will be concern that they also gave up 36 points to the Cats from the same source. Versatile big man Luke Jackson could be the key to the stoppage battle after he had a game-high eight clearances against the Cats. But the onball brigade of Hayden Young, Caleb Serong, Andrew Brayshaw, Murphy Reid and Bolton will test the Swans’ depth. The Dockers will be relieved their three-pronged tall forward set-up fired in their second final after Josh Treacy, Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss combined for two goals in the loss to the Hawks. The trio bounced back to share seven goals against that Cats as Voss led the way with four, and their ability to take marks inside 50 will be important to setting up their own opportunities as well as taking away the Swans’ rebound. Jonathan Horn brings expert analysis on the week's biggest AFL stories Errol Gulden: The Swans’ hard-running midfielder shouldered the load in the absence of five banned teammates in the stirring win over the Lions. The academy graduate has averaged 39 disposals, seven clearances and nine score involvements across his past six matches as he hits peak form at just the right time. The 24-year-old would have been closely considered to be stand-in skipper in place of Mills before former co-captain Dane Rampe received the nod. Gulden’s leadership can come out in other ways as he showed in response to the Lions’ inevitable surge, when he pulled off an incredible solo goal with a burst from the middle that ended with a snap to reclaim momentum for his side. The Swans might be lacking some star power but in Gulden they have a midfielder who can inspire the side like few others. Shai Bolton: The Dockers’ dynamo set the tone for his side’s emphatic response to their qualifying final horror show as he booted the opening two goals within as many minutes of the first ball-up against the Cats. The two-time All Australian finished with 26 disposals, four clearances and eight tackles as he adds more strings to his bow as a high-impact onballer. The 27-year-old’s link-up play helps the Dockers turn defence into attack while he remains a danger in the forward half where his pace and clever positioning helps him to average a goal a game. Bolton can expect to have James Rowbottom for company whenever he steps into the engine room, after the Swans’ tackling machine locked down on Lachie Neale in the qualifying final. Fremantle showed they can rise to the occasion with just their second finals victory since 2015 in a classic contest against Geelong. Sydney have proven they can win with their backs to the wall but, with the element of surprise now gone in how they want to play finals and their captain’s injury adding to their concerns, a clash with the minor premiers looks a step too far for the undermanned side.

title: Porsche’s Most Reliable Cayenne Is Currently Selling For New Honda CR-V Money - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update Depreciation is one of the automotive world's great equalizers. A luxury SUV that was once well beyond reach can, after a few years on the road, land squarely in the same price bracket as a brand-new mainstream crossover — and that's exactly the situation buyers find themselves in today with the third-generation Porsche Cayenne. The 2019 model year, which kicked off that generation, has depreciated to the point where well-priced examples trade for roughly the same money as a new Honda CR-V. The gap in prestige, performance, and interior quality between the two, however, remains enormous. We're taking a closer look at the 2019 Porsche Cayenne and its reliability record, comparing it with a new CR-V in terms of running costs and features. If you're on the hunt for wallet-friendly luxury, this might be the right choice for you. 3.0L turbo V6 / 2.9L twin-turbo V6 / 4.0L twin-turbo V8 / 3.0L V6 + 1 electric motor The 2019 Porsche Cayenne was the very first model year of the Cayenne's third generation, which had been revealed two years earlier. The model is built on Volkswagen's MLB platform, which it shares with several other models in the Volkswagen Group. These include the Audi Q7 and Q8, the Bentley Bentayga, the Volkswagen Touareg, and the Lamborghini Urus. The third-gen Cayenne's design evolved rather than revolutionized its predecessor's look, with revised door surfacing, a reworked front end, and a lowered roofline that lends the SUV a noticeably sportier stance. The signature teardrop headlight shape carried over unchanged. Four powertrain options are available for the 2019 model. The base trim runs a 3.0-liter turbocharged V6 producing 335 hp, while the Cayenne S steps up to a 2.9-liter twin-turbo V6 good for 434 hp. At the top of the naturally aspirated range sits the Turbo, whose 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 delivers 541 hp. Rounding out the lineup is the Cayenne E-Hybrid, which pairs the 3.0-liter V6 with an electric motor for a combined 455 hp. All variants use an eight-speed automatic transmission. The 2019 Cayenne's interior is, as expected, plush and comfortable, with plenty of tech on board (although, of course, this is now seven-year-old tech, so you can't exactly expect 2026-level features). The most interesting aspect of the Cayenne's cabin is the level of customization on offer when it comes to colors and materials. Of course, this doesn't really apply when shopping for a used car, but it does mean you are likely to run into a wide range of interior configurations when browsing through listings: the sheer number of options made available to customers when the model was released means that no two Cayennes are exactly the same. The infotainment system is controlled via a 12.3-inch touchscreen. Thanks to the Porsche Connect Plus system, there is a mobile Wi-Fi hotspot on board, as well as Apple CarPlay connectivity (but not Android Auto). Some models are equipped with the optional rear seat entertainment package, which adds a further two 10-inch screens on the back of the front seats. Shopping for a 2019 Porsche Cayenne on the used market means navigating an exceptionally wide price range. Mileage, service history, and trim level all play significant roles in determining asking price, with Turbo variants commanding the highest figures. The lower end of the range sits around the $24,000 mark, while the upper end is around $65,000. A substantial number of 2019 Cayennes for sale today are roughly equal in price to a brand new Honda CR-V, which starts at $32,370 and goes up to $36,850. Despite being the first year of a new generation, the 2019 Cayenne has a great reputation for reliability. The third-gen model has earned itself the top spot in CarBuzz's ranking of Cayenne generations according to reliability, as there are very few issues associated with it. That said, as with any vehicle, a handful of problem areas are worth monitoring. The most frequently reported concerns include squeaky brakes, lurching and surging transmissions, and vibration at higher speeds — the latter being largely confined to V6-powered examples. The 2019 model achieves a JD Power Quality and Reliability score of 79/100. According to the NHTSA, it has accumulated only 33 complaints and is associated with six recalls — a respectable record for a model now in its seventh year of life. The most frequent culprits in the NHTSA complaints database are the airbags, electrical systems, and driver assistance features such as forward collision avoidance. As long as careful, regular maintenance is performed according to schedule, your 2019 Cayenne is unlikely to experience major issues, and should provide you with many years of trouble-free ownership. While the 2019 Cayenne has a great reputation for reliability, and the 2026 Honda CR-V is a brand-new vehicle (meaning mechanical issues are highly unlikely), we have still taken a look at expected running costs for both models. This will help give you a more complete picture of what you can expect in terms of ownership experience from two models that have roughly the same upfront cost, but are very different in nature. We have made an estimate of what each model's approximate running costs are, based on a variety of sources including RepairPal, Edmunds, Porsche, and Honda. For the 2019 Cayenne, expect annual maintenance costs of around $1,200, with average repair costs over the first five years of ownership sitting near the $8,700 mark. By contrast, a brand-new Honda CR-V is projected to cost as little as $100 in maintenance during the first year, with that figure not expected to exceed $1,000 until after year three. First-five-year repair costs for the CR-V are estimated at around $900. Average fuel costs are also going to be much lower for the CR-V, which achieves a fuel economy of 28/34/30 MPG against the 2019 Cayenne's 19/23/21 MPG. Although insurance costs depend on a multitude of different factors, all other things being equal you can also expect to pay much less to insure a new Honda CR-V than a 2019 Cayenne, as the latter is a more powerful and luxurious vehicle. If, however, these increased costs are not a barrier to ownership for you, and you think the opportunity to get a luxury SUV at a reduced price is an acceptable trade-off, then a 2019 Porsche Cayenne could be your perfect used car purchase. The Honda CR-V might have lower running costs compared to a used Cayenne, but opting for a brand-new car is a surefire way to lose money in the long run. The 2019 Cayenne is most likely going to keep depreciating over the next few years before finding a plateau to settle on — buying a 2026 CR-V means a guaranteed loss of thousands of dollars before you even finish paying the loan off. According to CarEdge, CR-Vs depreciate by an average of 29% after the first five years on the road. That's pretty good when compared to other new SUVs. CarEdge assumes an average new purchase price of $38,131 when including available options, which equates to a five-year used price of $27,069. Most new cars lose value quickly in the first few years on the road, then the rate at which value drops slows considerably. The same source explains how a CR-V will cost you an average of $36,935 over the course of its first five years on the road. Here's how that breaks down: Buyers can contemplate the differences between these two models all day — luxury vs economy, style vs blending in, etc. However, none of that means much if you can't afford to protect your asset in the worst-case scenario of a crash or other incident after buying it. Some may feel like insurance is a scam when they consider how much money they pay every month, only to have to argue for coverage when you need it, but having it is the law, and it will come in handy one day. It's no surprise the Porsche Cayenne is more expensive to insure than a Honda CR-V. According to The Zebra, Cayennes cost an average of $1,333 for a six-month policy, which comes out to about $222 per month for the average driver with no recent accidents. On the flip side, average buyers with good driving records only pay about $796 for a six-month policy on a CR-V, which comes out to $133 per month. A comparison between a luxury car and a more affordable one is always going to have limited usefulness, as the two models live in very different areas of the automotive world. However, since depreciation has now brought the 2019 Cayenne's price point down to the level of the 2026 CR-V, we are highlighting a few areas where the Cayenne has the upper hand despite its age. Wide variety of interior styles and features: The 2019 Cayenne was a highly customizable model when released. As a result, the vehicles you will find on sale today have a veritable rainbow of interior colors and materials on board. There is something out there for every driver, from understated beige and black to bright neon green. Luxury and comfort: Being a high-end vehicle, the 2019 Cayenne will surpass even a brand new Honda CR-V in terms of plushness. While the CR-V is stylish, comfortable, and practical for its price point, the quality of the materials and design will be very different from that of a luxury car, even a seven-year-old one. Performance: The two models are in completely separate classes on the performance front, with the Cayenne's base model outpacing the CR-V by nearly 150 horsepower. Even the V6-powered Cayenne dispatches 0–60 mph in around five seconds, while the CR-V takes somewhere between 7.5 and 8 seconds to complete the same run. The top speed gap is equally stark: around 130 mph for the CR-V versus approximately 165 mph for the Cayenne. While there is nothing wrong with buying a used Cayenne, or a new CR-V, for that matter, shelling out for an SUV could be seen as a little safe and boring these days. It's what everyone drives, so for anyone wanting something that genuinely feels a bit special and different — without compromising on practicality and usability — perhaps a Panamera is the more suitable choice. Hailing from the same years, the Panamera shares much in common with the Cayenne. This is a good thing: as explained above, the powertrains are largely reliable, running costs aren't crippling, and the real good news is that depreciation has played its part here, too. Much in the same way that a 2019 Cayenne can be secured for around $25,000 to $35,000, a Panamera of a similar vintage can be netted for a comparable sum. Our price trends tool shows that 2017, 2018, and 2019 models all hover around $40,000 on average. Naturally, higher-mileage examples will drop comfortably into the $30,000s, while higher-spec grades command significantly more. It's not a sensible decision, per se, but it does come with a Porsche badge and everything that represents — quality, performance, and prestige — and the sensible Honda simply cannot compete on those terms. title: Brentford v Chelsea - Match Preview, kick-off time and more - Brentford FC
content: Analysis, team news, match officials and more - here's everything you need to know ahead of the game. Xabi Alonso's Chelsea visit Gtech Community Stadium on Friday for a west London derby under the lights - and the early-season numbers point towards an intriguing meeting between two attacking sides who create chances easily. Now 44, Alonso racked up 143 Premier League appearances during five seasons at Liverpool between 2004 and 2009, and he is back in the English top flight after a stellar start to his managerial career with Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid. Alonso's return to England has certainly been entertaining: his four Premier League games in the Chelsea dugout have yielded 19 goals at either end - more than those of any other team so far this term. Currently on seven points, the Blues sit a point ahead of unbeaten Brentford in the table, with much of the pre-match attention likely to centre on Chelsea's new-look front three of Cole Palmer, João Pedro and Morgan Rogers. The Blues' attacking trio has amassed a combined eight goals and six assists already this term, with Rogers slotting in seamlessly after the £117 million switch from Aston Villa that made him the most expensive English player in history. Dig a little further back into the Premier League archives and the threat posed by Palmer-João Pedro-Rogers snaps even more sharply into focus. Dating back to the start of the 2024/25 season, João Pedro has 42 Premier League goal involvements (28G, 14A), Rogers has 38 (21G, 17A) and Palmer has 37 (27G, 10A). That's a combined 76 goals and 41 assists, with the trio's creative threat further underlined by all three ranking in the division’s top 20 for key passes this season. Brentford, however, have been lively in attack themselves, scoring 15 goals in domestic competition this season - only Chelsea (18) have managed more among Premier League teams. The Bees have also played a lower percentage of their passes backwards (13.3 per cent) than any other side in the top flight in 2026/27, an indication of the attacking intent that has characterised their unbeaten start. Crucially, neither side has needed to dominate possession to create opportunities. Brentford (17 per 90) rank third in the Premier League for shots this term, while Chelsea lead the division for shots on target (six per 90) - despite both the Bees (46 per cent) and the Blues (44 per cent) averaging under 50 per cent of possession. Where the two sides differ slightly is in how those opportunities have been created. Chelsea have been particularly dangerous on the break, leading the Premier League for shots (10) and goals (three) on the counter this term, while Brentford top the division for shots inside the six-yard box (nine) and shots from set-pieces (30). Both sides will enter the contest knowing how they can hurt one another - the interesting part will be seeing who can execute best on the night. Hopes for 2025/26 were high after Enzo Maresca’s side won the Conference League, the Club World Cup and returned to the top four in the Premier League the season before. But their start was nothing to write home about and, across the last seven league games of 2025, they won just once. That victory came against Everton on 13 December and, afterwards, Maresca said: “The last 48 hours have been the worst 48 hours since I joined the club because many people didn’t support us.” There had reportedly been a breakdown in relationships behind the scenes. The 2-2 draw at home to Bournemouth on 30 December proved to be Maresca’s last - and on New Year’s Day, he left by mutual consent. U21 coach Calum McFarlane took over in the interim, before Liam Rosenior left Chelsea’s sister club Strasbourg to sign a six-and-a-half-year deal at Stamford Bridge on 6 January. At first, the change seemed to have worked a treat. Despite losing to neighbours Fulham in his first Premier League game, Rosenior oversaw four straight wins and lost only two of his first nine. But from 14 March to 21 April, the Blues lost five consecutive league games without scoring - their worst run without a goal since 1912. He was sacked on 22 April, just over three months after taking the job. McFarlane assumed control again for the remainder of the season and was in the dugout for the FA Cup final, which Chelsea lost 1-0 to Manchester City. They ultimately finished 10th, meaning a third season in four without Champions League football. One day after the defeat at Wembley, Xabi Alonso was appointed as the club’s new manager on a four-year contract. He had been out of work since January, when he left Real Madrid, but his success at Bayer Leverkusen before that - particularly the unbeaten season in the Bundesliga - spoke for itself. Chelsea’s hierarchy knew that and wholeheartedly backed him in the summer. He reportedly wanted to add experience and know-how, so veterans Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson came in - and so did more than £330m worth of new talent. Morgan Rogers’ £117m move from Aston Villa - an all-time record for an English player - made up more than a third of that. They sold Enzo Fernández to Man City for £125m, too, but a deal for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, who was viewed as his replacement, fell through on Deadline Day. Regardless, Alonso later said he was “happy” with the state of his squad. Rogers’ arrival has made Chelsea’s frontline - along with Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto and João Pedro - one of the most fearsome in the Premier League; they already have nine league goals and six assists between them. Without European football to compete in this season, if they keep up such ferocity in front of goal, Alonso has the ingredients to make the club serious contenders again. A return to Europe should be a formality. But then again, there is never a dull moment at Chelsea. Born in Spain’s Basque Country, Xabi Alonso started out at Antiguoko, the club that produced fellow Premier League managers Mikel Arteta and Andoni Iraola. Back then, the club acted as a feeder club to Real Sociedad and, in 1999, Alonso joined the San Sebastián-based team for whom his dad - former Spain international Periko Alonso - played between 1977 and 1982. He made his debut in the Copa del Rey in November 1999 and went on to play 124 times before signing for Liverpool in 2004. Over the next five seasons on Merseyside, Alonso played over 200 games and scored the goal that sent the 2005 Champions League final against AC Milan to extra-time, before the Reds won on penalties to complete what became known as ‘The Miracle of Istanbul’. He left for Real Madrid in 2009 and, while at the Bernabéu, won one La Liga title, two Copa del Reys and the 2013/14 Champions League. Alonso closed out his career at Bayern Munich, where he won three straight Bundesliga titles under Pep Guardiola, before announcing his retirement in March 2017 on Twitter, with his famous “Lived it. Loved it” post. The following year, he began his journey into coaching with Real Madrid’s U14s, before he returned to Sociedad in June 2019 as the B team manager and guided them to promotion to the Segunda Division in 2020/21. He left in the summer of 2022 and moved back to Germany to take over at Bayer Leverkusen. In his first season at the BayArena, Leverkusen finished sixth - but in his second, they won their first-ever Bundesliga title by winning 28 of their 34 league games and not losing a single one. They also won their first DFB-Pokal since 1992/93 and finished as runners-up in the Europa League. Alonso returned to Real Madrid after the 2024/25 season but lasted only until January 2026, when he left by mutual consent. Four months later, he signed a four-year deal to take over at Chelsea. Bobby Vincent, senior football correspondent for Mirror Sport and football.london, explains how Chelsea are likely to be set up against the Bees. "It is a difficult one to predict because Alonso has kept us guessing with either 3-4-3 or 4-2-3-1. I would expect the former," he told brentfordfc.com. "That is what we have seen more of in the early part of the season. It allows Chelsea to have plenty of players in attacking positions but, as we have seen so far this season, the Blues are susceptible to being counter attacked." Last Premier League starting XI v Chelsea (4-2-3-1): Martínez; Gusto, Fofana, Colwill, Hato; James, Lavia; Pedro Neto, Palmer, Rogers; João Pedro Josh Dasilva (hamstring), Antoni Milambo (ACL), Nathan Collins (calf), Sepp van den Berg (groin) and Kaye Furo (metatarsal) remain sidelined for Brentford. Andrew Madley will be the man in the middle for Friday night's game against Chelsea. It will be his third Premier League referee appointment of the season, with him previously overseeing Crystal Palace against Manchester City and, most recently, Nottingham Forest's 2-1 victory at Aston Villa. Madley has had the whistle for 25 Brentford games in the past, with the Bees winning 10, drawing four and losing 11 of those clashes. A late equaliser from Fábio Carvalho secured a point for Brentford in a 2-2 draw against Chelsea at Gtech Community Stadium. The Bees took the lead through Kevin Schade in the first half, before Cole Palmer and Moisés Caicedo netted after half-time. But it was the Bees who had the final word in the west London derby, when Carvalho tucked in at the back post after a long throw-in had been flicked on by Kristoffer Ajer. title: AFL finals: where the Hawthorn v Brisbane preliminary final will be won and lost | Martin Pegan - The Guardian
content: The Hawks meet the modern-day Lions in a final for the first time as they aim to end the back-to-back premiers’ bid for a rare three-peat Hawthorn are well placed to make the leap into a first grand final since 2015 after building steadily across three finals campaigns and putting on a dominant qualifying final display. A victory over Brisbane at this stage could even be the first step in a changing of the guard. But the Lions surely won’t give up their crown without a fight, as they aim to become just the third VFL/AFL side in nearly seven decades – after an earlier version from each of these clubs – to claim a premiership three-peat. The Hawks could hardly have been more impressive as they ambushed the Dockers on their home turf to earn a week’s break and a home preliminary final at the MCG. The resounding triumph for Sam Mitchell’s side against the minor premiers came as a surprise to many but the signs were there in a hot streak that now includes one defeat in their past eight matches. The lingering concern will be that the loss in that stretch was a thumping from the Lions, who the Hawks have failed to beat in their past three clashes. The Lions are back on familiar ground in a fifth consecutive preliminary final – and at the same venue and in the same Saturday twilight slot as in the past two years when they not only secured a spot in a pair of grand finals but won back-to-back flags. Chris Fagan’s side is treading much the same path as last year when they were hammered in a qualifying final before bouncing back a week later. The Lions have done well to regenerate on the run but will have to knock down a Hawks side on the rise to earn a shot at joining the greatest teams of the modern era. Hawthorn have been the fourth-best side this season at limiting opposition scores but put on a defensive masterclass in their qualifying final win against the Dockers. With their pressure ramped up and a well-honed structure across the field they stifled the minor premiers’ ball movement and conceded only five goals from 57 inside-50s. The Hawks lost two of 20 matches when they held the opposition under 100 points this year. But their four other defeats came from the four times when they conceded 120 points or more. The Hawks’ defence might be integral to their success but they also have the firepower to hurt the Lions in attack. Evergreen Jack Gunston (61 goals) remains the focal point while a spread of pacey half-forwards link the play and offer their own threat near goal. Nick Watson (57) is the standout as arguably the best small forward in the game, but Dylan Moore, Jack Ginnivan and Connor Macdonald can hit the scoreboard and will be just as critical in pressuring the Lions’ at-times shaky defence. Brisbane have their own fleet of half-forwards who showed they still set the standard when they came out with a point to prove and blew away Adelaide. Veteran goalsneak Charlie Cameron (55 goals) leads the way while Kai Lohmann (48) has taken his game to another level. Zac Bailey and Cam Rayner are two of the most powerful front-half players in the competition and can also pinch-hit in the midfield. The spread of goal threats, even before considering young key forward Logan Morris (67), will test the Hawks’ defence and the ability for the likes of James Sicily to rebound off intercepts. The Lions can turn to greater depth of top-end talent in the midfield. Will Ashcroft has put together a season befitting of a two-time Norm Smith medallist, the injury-plagued Hugh McCluggage will be better for an extra game in the legs, and Josh Dunkley adds the balance with his defensive nous. Lachie Neale’s finals form is a mounting concern at the same time as the dual Brownlow medallist is reportedly heading for the exit. But the Lions’ onball brigade have proved over a long stretch they can rise to the occasion with contest and clearance dominance in a knockout final. Jonathan Horn brings expert analysis on the week's biggest AFL stories Will Day: The Hawks’ smooth-moving midfielder was made to wait for his finals debut after a long battle with injuries forced him out late in the 2024 and 2025 campaigns. The 25-year-old has enjoyed an uninterrupted run since putting foot and shoulder issues behind him and quickly showed he is made for the big stage with a sublime performance in the Hawks’ qualifying final. Day helped his side make the most of their early momentum before finishing with 24 disposals and eight clearances and let his emotions spill over on the final siren. Blessed with poise and polish, Day adds balance to the Hawks’ onball brigade and will be critical to his team’s chances against the Lions, especially with master-minder Dunkley likely to spend time by his side. Charlie Cameron: The livewire was one of several experienced Lions to have the blowtorch turned on them after a lacklustre qualifying final performance. The 32-year-old went goalless for just the second time this year in the defeat to the Swans but it was no surprise to see him spark the Lions in their emphatic response. Cameron booted a bag of five for the first time in more than two years in the semi-final to send another reminder that he is a big-game performer. The small forward has the second-most finals goals since the start of 2000 with 58, only behind Lance Franklin in that period – as much a reflection of his consistent impact as his durability. Cameron will play his 30th final this week for the 10th-most in VFL/AFL history and now has a fifth career grand final in his sights. Brisbane have been at the top of the mountain for so long they can be forgiven for the occasional insipid performance and have shown in recent years that when they switch on for a do-or-die clash they are almost unstoppable. Hawthorn are undeniably a team on the rise but for now will find the reigning premiers’ spread of talent too much to contain.

title: Statement of National Postal Mail Handlers Union National President Paul V. Hogrogian on the Supreme Court Decision on Vote by Mail - National Postal Mail Handlers Union
content: Time and time again, Mail Handlers and the United States Postal Service has shown its more than capable of delivering ballots to and from voters and local election officials. During the 2024 federal elections, over 99 million ballots were processed by the Postal Service. 99.8 percent of ballots were delivered to election officials within a week, and 97.73 percent were delivered within three days. Additionally, voter fraud is a non-issue in our democratic process. There is no evidence of overwhelming voter fraud that would actually impact the outcome of elections. The Heritage Foundation issued reports on voter fraud and found that during the 2024 elections, there were only forty-three cases of voter fraud that led to criminal conviction throughout the country. In 2020, there were thirty-one. The proposed rule and executive order that not only create excessive and unnecessary oversight on elections from the Postal Service, but overstepped the constitutional rights of states to administer elections. The NPMHU applauds the Supreme Court Justices that upheld this right and overturned the infringement on access to ballots through the mail. Vote by mail is a vital part of America’s democratic process that has been used for almost two hundred years. Eight states and the District of Columbia exclusively vote by mail. It is necessary for the elderly, invalid, those who work outside polling locations' hours, and voters who find themselves away from home during an election. A healthy democracy is dependent on all eligible voters participating. The National Postal Mail Handlers Union will continue to do our part in democracy to support vote by mail.

title: Larry V. Flint Obituary Sep 8, 2026 - Walker Funeral Homes & Crematory
content: Larry V. Flint, 66, of Toledo, Ohio, formerly of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, passed away on September 8, 2026. Born May 14, 1960 in Philadelphia to the late Esther Gibson-Flint and Lawrence Flint. Larry was educated within the Philadelphia public school system and earned his GED. He later enlisted and served his country in both the United States Army and the United States Navy. Following his honorable discharge, he returned home to serve his community as a Philadelphia Firefighter. Driven by a passion for cooking, Larry graduated from The Walnut Hill Culinary School. He later relocated to Toledo, Ohio, where he served for several years as a Culinary Specialist at Rosary Care Center, and concluded his career with the United States Postal Service. An avid history buff, Larry enjoyed a good debate no matter what the topic was. A proud Philadelphian at heart, he was a devoted sports fan and die-hard Philadelphia Eagles fan. Above all, he loved his family and he knew and loved the Lord. He was preceded in death by his parents and his sister, Cheryl Flint. He leaves to cherish his memory his beloved wife, Stephanie Potter-Flint; his son, Lawrence C. Flint; daughters, Lauren V. Flint, Jasmine Jackson, and Breanna Stewart; granddaughters, Imani Flint, Chloe Jackson, and Gabriella "Gabby" Evans; brother, Gregory Gibson of Philadelphia; sisters, Terri (Alto King) of Toledo, Ohio and Lydia (Butch Ifill) of Philadelphia; and a host of beloved nieces, nephews, extended family and friends. title: CDT Files Amicus Brief in Meta Platforms v. Bonta - Center for Democracy and Technology
content: CDT works on a wide range of issues where technology shapes our fundamental rights and freedoms. Imagine a customer walking into a bookstore. She loves mysteries and just finished a great book. She wants something along the same lines but she doesn’t know what, so she asks the bookseller. The bookseller considers their inventory, directs her to the non-fiction section and to a specific title that she might like based on the last book she read. She may not have considered this book because it’s outside of the genre she has typically preferred, but the bookseller knew to recommend it based on what she had said, what the bookseller knew of the book, and other customers who had enjoyed it. A law that prohibited this interaction would have significant First Amendment implications. Yet that’s exactly what a law in California does, except for teenagers on social media. On September 15, 2026, the Center for Democracy & Technology and Electronic Frontier Foundation filed an amicus brief along with the Wikimedia Foundation in Meta Platforms v. Bonta, challenging California’s SB 976. CDT and EFF filed the brief to bring to the court’s attention the law’s broader impacts on young people’s freedom of expression and access to information online. The brief explains that personalized recommendation systems help users find information and audiences for their own speech, and that restricting teenagers’ access to those systems burdens their First Amendment rights. It further argues that platforms’ decisions about what content to recommend, to whom, and in what order are protected editorial judgments, even when those decisions are implemented through automated systems. Finally, the brief explains that recognizing these First Amendment protections does not prevent states from addressing legitimate concerns about the addictive nature of these recommendation systems and the private surveillance that drives them. States can pursue more narrowly tailored approaches, including stronger privacy protections and tools that give young people greater control over the content they see, without broadly restricting their ability to use personalized recommendations. title: X Corp. v. Operation Bluebird, Inc.: When Is a Trademark Truly Abandoned? - JD Supra
content:
Rebranding is serious business. The associated risks and costs are often substantial, and the decision to overhaul marketplace identity should never be taken lightly. Organizations must consider the potential loss of established goodwill, particularly during the period of transition from old to new. Consumer perception of the brand may change, and brand awareness may falter. A new trademark must be cleared, and consumers must be educated to look for the new brand name, logo, or slogan. To maximize the benefits and minimize the risks of a rebrand, companies often devote a significant amount of effort and resources to the creation and maintenance of the new brand. However, as demonstrated by the recent memorandum opinion in X Corp. v. Operation Bluebird, Inc., No. 25-1510-CFC (D. Del. Sept. 3, 2026), there are additional risks associated with rebranding that may not be immediately apparent. Notably, entities must be conscious of what constitutes trademark abandonment to prevent others from attempting to capitalize on the goodwill associated with the old brand. In 2006, Twitter, Inc. launched the social media internet platform known as Twitter. Between 2006 and 2023, millions of people accessed Twitter through the Internet website twitter.com, short message service, and mobile-device application software to share and comment on short messages known as “tweets.”[1] Twitter, Inc. filed 13 separate trademark applications with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Eight of these applications featured the term “TWITTER,” either by itself or in connection with additional wording (the “TWITTER-formative marks”). Two applications featured the term “TWEET.” The remaining three applications featured a design mark known as the Twitter Bird logo.[2] In March 2023, X Corp. acquired Twitter, Inc.’s assets, including the referenced 13 trademarks.[3] X Corp. then rebranded the Twitter platform to “X” in July 2023 and adopted a stylized version of the letter X as the platform’s new mark.[4] As part of the rebrand, X Corp. removed from the platform the Twitter Bird logo design and all references to the terms “Twitter” and “Tweet.”[5] In December 2025, Operation Bluebird, Inc. (Bluebird) filed two intent-to-use trademark applications with the USPTO to register the marks “TWITTER” and “TWEET,” and announced its intent to launch a social networking platform called “twitter.new.”[6] The backdrop of the twitter.new home page featured the same sky-blue color of twitter.com’s old backdrop and the Twitter Bird logo. By December 22, 2025, over 140,000 people had reserved usernames on the platform.[7] X Corp. sued Bluebird for alleged trademark infringement and trademark dilution, among other claims.[8] X Corp. then filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to enjoin Bluebird from using the TWITTER marks referenced above until the case is resolved and argued that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its infringement and dilution claims.[9] In response, Bluebird argued that X Corp. cannot prevail on such claims because X Corp. deliberately abandoned and thus no longer owns any rights in the TWITTER marks.[10] The Lanham Act states that a mark shall be deemed “abandoned” when use of the mark has been discontinued with intent not to resume such use.[11] Intent not to resume may be inferred from circumstances. Accordingly, the Court applied a two-part inquiry to determine whether X Corp. abandoned its TWITTER marks: In analyzing X Corp.’s motion for a preliminary injunction, the Court framed the relevant question as “whether Bluebird has shown that it is likely to succeed in strictly proving at trial that X Corp. does not use and intends not to resume using the TWITTER marks.”[13] With respect to the eight TWITTER-formative marks, the Court determined that Bluebird had not made that showing. The Court focused on the following evidence of record: (1) language found in X Corp.’s online listing for its downloadable software application that stated “Welcome to X (formerly known as Twitter)”; (2) testimony from a Legal Director at X Corp. that indicated the listing language was deliberately added to ensure consumers who were searching for the Twitter application would understand that X Corp.’s product was one and the same; and (3) survey evidence demonstrating that the TWITTER mark is “well-known, commercially strong, and famous among the general consuming public in the United States.”[14] The Court found that X Corp.’s use of the wording “formerly Twitter” in a listing designed to advertise and promote the X platform constituted evidence of bona fide use of the TWITTER-formative marks.[15] With respect to the marks featuring the term TWEET or the Twitter Bird logo, however, the Court determined that Bluebird is likely to succeed in strictly proving that X Corp. has discontinued bona fide use of the marks.[16] Neither the term “TWEET” or the Twitter Bird logo appear in the listing of the X app on the Apple App Store, and X Corp. conceded that these marks are nowhere to be found on X Corp.’s home page.[17] The Court reviewed other evidence provided by X Corp. to prove use of such marks, such as an email to solicit the services of a potential vendor, older webpage materials, and legacy (“inactive”) social media accounts bearing the marks.[18] However, the Court determined X Corp.’s evidence to be “remnants of prior use” that did not show that X Corp. is “currently engaged in the bona fide use” of the relevant marks.[19] The Court further determined that Bluebird is likely to succeed in proving that X Corp. has no intent to resume use of the TWEET or Twitter Bird logo marks and thus is likely to strictly prove abandonment of such marks.[20] In reaching its conclusion, the Court referenced statements made by Elon Musk, the owner of X Corp., indicating that his intention was to “cut[] the Twitter logo off the building with blow torches.”[21] Per the Court’s opinion, “Musk’s pronouncements and X Corp.’s rebranding of the Twitter platform as X provide compelling evidence that X Corp. harbors an intent not to resume use of the Tweet mark and Bird logo.”[22] Trademark abandonment is a potential consequence of any rebranding exercise. However, an entity may employ several strategies to protect the goodwill associated with its “old” and “new” brands. As demonstrated by the opinion in X Corp. v. Operation Bluebird, Inc., use of the term “formerly” in advertising is a key factor in determining whether an entity has abandoned its mark. Even though it may be clear to consumers that the relevant goods or services are now being provided under a new mark, a reference to the previous source identifier in promotions for the new brand may be sufficient to defeat the defense of abandonment.[23] This also helps entities to capitalize on and transfer the goodwill established by the prior mark to the new mark. However, if an entity is unable to demonstrate any use or reference to the “old” brand in current advertising or marketing materials, there is a risk of trademark abandonment. A third party may attempt to capitalize on the goodwill associated with the former mark by providing similar goods or services under such a mark, and it may be difficult for the original mark owner to succeed in proving trademark infringement or dilution. Therefore, before proceeding with a rebrand, it is important to consult with a trademark attorney that can advise on potential risks, develop strategies to protect the established goodwill of the brand, and ensure a smooth transition from old to new. [1] X Corp. v. Operation Bluebird, Inc., No. 25-1510-CFC, slip op. at 2-3 (D. Del. Sept. 3, 2026). [8]Id. at 2. X Corp. sued Bluebird for alleged trademark infringement, counterfeiting, false designation of origin and unfair competition, trademark dilution, and copyright infringement in violation of federal law and common law trademark infringement and unfair competition, deceptive trade practices, and trademark dilution in violation of Delaware law. [12]X Corp. v. Operation Bluebird, Inc., No. 25-1510-CFC, slip op. at 9 (D. Del. Sept. 3, 2026). [23]See, e.g., Wells Fargo & Co. v. ABD Ins. & Fin. Servs., 758 F.3d 1069, 1072 (9th Cir. 2014); Marks Org., Inc. v. Joles, 784 F. Supp. 2d 322, 328 (S.D.N.Y. 2011); Perry v. H.J. Heinz Co. Brands, L.L.C., 994 F.3d 466, 475 (5th Cir. 2021). title: First Virginia Payload Module (VPM) Spotted for U.S. Navy’s Block V Submarines - navalnews.com
content: Home » First Virginia Payload Module (VPM) Spotted for U.S. Navy’s Block V Submarines General Dynamics Electric Boat has shared a photo showing the first completed Virginia Payload Module (VPM) for the U.S. Navy’s Block V submarines, expanding strike capacity. General Dynamics Electric Boat posted the first view of the future USS Arizona’s (SSGN-803) Virginia Payload Module (VPM) on Monday, September 14. The completed section is seen floating on a barge, presumably beginning transport towards final assembly at GD Electric Boat’s facility in Groton, Connecticut. The USS Arizona will represent the first submarine in U.S. Navy inventory equipped with the VPM, despite being the second Block V boat to enter service, following the USS Oklahoma (SSN-802). She represents the first of 19 total hulls fitted with the VPM, with a total of 12 Block Vs and 7 Block VI hulls receiving the upgrade over the course of the next two decades. The sighting of the first fully constructed VPM marks a key milestone in returning and ensuring critical strike capabilities across the undersea fleet. The VPM will give the USS Arizona a more than 3x increase in Vertical Launch Cell capacity over previous hulls, with up to 28 additional Tomahawk-sized missiles carried in four larger canisters housing seven missiles apiece. This increases the VLS missile allotment to 40 when accounting for the two Virginia Payload tubes carried in the bow with six missiles apiece. Alternatively, each canister can carry three Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) hypersonic boost-glide weapons, with the Navy utilizing the same mounting systems for CPS present on the Zumwalt-class destroyers following their conversions. Each of the 19 VPM-equipped submarines will be 83 feet longer than their sisters, with a completed VPM constituting roughly 184 out of 460 feet of total length. Each of these 19 submarines will retain upgrades administered to earlier blocks, including a new side-mounted sonar array first found with the construction of the Block V boats. Currently, the first four Ohio-class submarines make up most of the U.S. submarine fleet’s conventional VLS capacity, with each submarine converted to carry 154 Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles in lieu of a complement of 16 Trident Submarine-Launched Ballistic Missiles in the early 2000s, letting the four boats dodge an early retirement. Consequently, a massive gap in conventional VLS capacity looms over the U.S. submarine fleet as each of the 40+ year-old converted Ohios begin to depart service. The VPM-equipped Virginias will thus backfill the capacity left behind by the Ohios, distributing missile capacity better across an increased number of modern platforms, with the U.S. Navy receiving an overall increase in VLS cells available once all of the VPM-equipped submarines are in service. Despite this, it remains unclear when the USS Arizona and the rest of her larger sisters will begin to reach U.S. Navy hands, as only the first VPM module is complete and awaits assembly alongside the rest of the submarine’s key compartments. VPM might also increase the flexibility of U.S. Navy attack submarines in the future, as the Navy increasingly seeks different types of munitions employed from submarine-mounted VLS tubes. In particular, Naval News has previously covered efforts to mount a submarine-launched variant of the AARGM-ER anti-radiation missile, bringing an explicit radar-hunting capability to U.S. submarines. Additionally, The War Zone reported on an effort to bring anti-air capabilities to submarines via a specific variant of the Navy Modular Missile (the Navy’s prospective next-generation interceptor), presumably meant to be utilized from undersea vertical launch systems. title: Viral Kid Podcasters Hen-Dawg and Jimmy V Make Their TODAY Debut and Admit: Just ‘Watched the Show Yesterday To Be Honest’ - TODAY.com
content:
Steals & Deals: Up to 80% Off Foldable Vacuums, Luggage Trackers, More Genius Gadgets Viral Kid Podcasters Hen-Dawg and Jimmy V Make Their TODAY Debut and Admit: Just ‘Watched the Show Yesterday To Be Honest’ For one new trending podcast, no topic is off limits: mental health, Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce, things that are “dead,” fantasy football and the top five lunch “pulls.” Henry “Hen-Dawg” Zotti and Jimmy “V” Maley, both 10, are using their growing platform to bring candid and authentic conversations from the next generation to the podcasting space. Their following of 12,000 and growing has taken them to the New York Times and gotten them noticed by Chicago Bears’ quarterback Caleb Williams, who gifted them a signed copy of the newest Madden videogame. When they stopped by TODAY on Sept. 16, they revealed to Craig Melvin, Savannah Guthrie and Jenna Bush Hager what it’s like working with your best friend and how they convinced their parents to let them take the mic. Like on their own show, Jimmy V did not hesitate to be authentic with viewers. “I watched this show yesterday, to be honest,” the 10-year-old guest admitted. “Just yesterday?” Jenna asked. “Had you ever seen it before?” “I have since I found out that I was on it,” Jimmy V said. Their podcast came to be when Jimmy V’s dad, who runs the mental health podcast “The Maley Way,” started letting them film their conversations just for fun. “We bugged my dad, almost too much,” Jimmy V said to Craig when asked how they got started with the podcast. “(Jimmy V’s dad) put the phone there, and then just let us do it,” Hen-Dawg added. The biggest creative disagreement they’ve run into? The Chicago Cubs versus the Chicago White Socks. Otherwise, the young co-hosts enjoy debating things like their favorite foods, which they did on-air. In ranking breakfast foods, Hen-Dawg’s ranking of chocolate chip pancakes at No. 5 mustered up quite the shocked face from Jimmy V, who almost jumped up from the sofa when Hen-Dawg placed bacon in fourth. Savannah gave Hen-Dawg a chance to defend his controversial choices. “I feel like bacon can just be too crispy sometimes,” Hen-Dawg said. “Or it can be not crispy. I need it to be just right, always.” “That’s how Mister Roker likes his bacon,” Craig shared. What the two could agree on is the elite nature of Lucky Charms — with just the marshmallows. “Respect!” Jimmy V exclaimed as he went in for their signature handshake, which often appears after they find common ground in their rankings. A few segments later, Craig and Savannah checked on the boys, who were found in the control room doing one of their favorite activities: snacking. The celebrity visitors, with headsets on, enjoyed some french-fries and Lucky Charms as they reclined in the production seats and watched more of the show. “That’s how our newsroom eats every day,” Savannah said. “I found it!” Hen-Dawg yelled, holding up his prized marshmallow. “Ok good, thank goodness,” Savannah said as the podcasters continued their charmed hunt. “Alright lil’ bros.” Jimmy V and Hen-Dawg returned to Studio 1A to chat more, as Dylan Dreyer and Al Roker joined in on the chance to chat with the new stars. The boys spoke highly of their newfound stardom and their appearance on TODAY. “I feel like you guys are really leaning into the perks of the TODAY show,” Dylan said, as the boys, who spent commercial breaks teaching the crew about fantasy football, enjoyed the spinning desk chairs. The boys finished their chat by ranking their Christmas lists. Jimmy V painted a very specific picture. “This might be a big ask, I want to get a framed, signed Ben Johnson, with the picture of the interview when he had his shirt off.” Georgie Gassaro is an editorial intern for TODAY.com and an Ithaca College journalism student. © 2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLCApple®, Apple logo® and App Store® are registered trademarks of Apple Inc. title: Honda HR-V vs Kia Seltos, a budget SUV Edmunds comparison - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
content: The 2027 Honda HR-V and 2027 Kia Seltos are two small SUVs that are easy to live with, offer enough room for everyday duties, keep fuel costs in check, and are versatile enough to be useful for a range of needs Crossovers have become a popular choice for buyers who want the practicality of an SUV without the size and expense of a larger vehicle. For many shoppers, that means finding a vehicle that’s easy to live with, offers enough room for everyday duties, keeps fuel costs in check, and provides the versatility to be useful for a range of needs. The 2027 Honda HR-V and 2027 Kia Seltos both make a case for that balance, but they take somewhat different approaches to the formula. Honda’s HR-V is the little sibling to the larger CR-V and sets a benchmark for what to expect from an extra-small SUV. Kia’s Seltos is less well known but enters 2027 with a full redesign that brings more space, revamped styling and a newly available hybrid powertrain. Both are compelling options, but which one is the better buy? Edmunds put these two SUVs head-to-head to find out. Both the Kia Seltos and Honda HR-V make good use of their compact dimensions, offering roomy cabins with generous space in both rows. The Seltos has an especially accommodating rear seat, even for taller passengers. Easy-access child seat anchors add to its family-friendly appeal. For a small SUV like this, the Seltos also boasts a reasonably smooth ride over bumps. The HR-V is similarly roomy, with large door openings and a comfortable seat height that make entry and exit a breeze. It also has a pretty smooth ride. But Edmunds noticed a difference in seat comfort between these two SUVs. The HR-V’s overly firm front seat cushions and lack of lumbar adjustment take a toll on long-distance comfort. If you frequently have rear passengers, the Seltos has another advantage by way of its rear air vents. You don’t get them in the HR-V. Neither the 158-horsepower Honda HR-V nor the 147-horsepower Kia Seltos is quick off the line. In Edmunds’ testing, the HR-V needed 10.2 seconds to get from zero to 60 mph, while the Seltos posted a 10.6-second run to 60 mph. Thankfully, you can get a Seltos with a more powerful 190-horsepower turbocharged engine that livens up the car’s acceleration. The HR-V is only available with its base engine. Both SUVs can deliver impressive fuel economy. The EPA estimates that the HR-V will get up to 28 mpg in combined city/highway driving. The Seltos gets up to an estimated 30 mpg combined, though the available turbocharged engine drops to 26 mpg combined. There’s not much of a difference here, but the upcoming hybrid-powered version of the Seltos could tip the scales later this year. The Seltos offers 27.8 cubic feet of cargo capacity behind the second row and up to 64.2 cubic feet with the rear seats folded, putting it among the roomiest vehicles in its class. Front storage is less impressive since the narrow center console is deep but not particularly spacious, but there are plenty of additional compartments for smaller items. The HR-V offers less capacity behind the rear seats at 24.4 cubic feet, but the cargo area is well thought out and makes good use of the space. The rear seatbacks fold nearly flat with the cargo floor, making it easier to haul longer items while expanding total cargo room to 55.1 cubic feet. Cabin storage is adequate, with a rubberized bridge compartment behind the shifter for wireless charging and a deep center-armrest bin, though the door pockets and glovebox are smaller than we’d prefer. The HR-V makes a strong impression with a well-built, thoughtfully designed interior that features soft-touch surfaces and high-quality-feeling controls. It’s also reasonably priced, with the HR-V LX trim starting at $28,150 including destination fees. The HR-V EX-L tops the lineup at $32,000. The Seltos has a lower starting price of $26,485, and while fully loaded trims can approach $40,000, you’re generally getting more for your money here. The Seltos has a bigger standard touchscreen, more available driver aids, and more convenience features — such as a power-adjustable driver’s seat or leather upholstery — at a lower price. Kia also has a significant advantage in warranty coverage, with five years/60,000 miles of basic coverage and 10 years/100,000 miles on the powertrain. The Honda HR-V covers the bases for what’s expected from an extra-small SUV. But the redesigned Kia Seltos has raised the bar to an all-new level with its generous passenger and cargo space, range of powertrain options, and appealing value. If you want top versatility and style from a small SUV, the Seltos is the way to go. This story was provided to The Associated Press by the automotive website Edmunds. Bradley Iger is a contributor at Edmunds.

title: Texas won’t release first maternal death report since overturning of Roe v. Wade until after midterms - Houston Public Media
content: The report, which has traditionally been released every other year on or near Sept. 1 will now not be released until Dec. 1. The Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) announced last week that it would not release its biannual maternal mortality report until December, pushing the release date to after the November election. The report, which had traditionally been released every other year on or near Sept. 1, was expected to contain the first full year of data on maternal mortality in the state since its near-total abortion ban went into effect. Texas officially banned nearly all abortions in August 2022, just two months after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. One year prior, in 2021, the state had passed the Texas Heartbeat Act, which banned any abortions at six weeks. Researchers, such as Faith Fletcher, a public health and bioethics expert, said the report provides essential data. "We need the data so that we can understand why women are dying [and] what are some solutions that we can propose," Fletcher told Houston Public Media. Fletcher, along with Kari White — a nonresident fellow in maternal and reproductive health at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy — authored an opinion in the Houston Chronicle last week criticizing DSHS's decision to push back the release date. Fletcher said the report will be key to understanding what effect the state's abortion ban has had on maternal health. "Based on what the trends have been, yes, we did expect an increase [in maternal mortality], but without having the comprehensive data specifically in Texas, it's hard to really make those assumptions," Fletcher said. In Texas, Black and Hispanic women are disproportionately impacted by maternal deaths, Fletcher said. "Generally speaking, from a national level, we know that many of these deaths are preventable — approximately 80%," Fletcher said. "This is generally what we see: lack of health insurance and adequate postpartum support, mental health conditions, intimate partner violence. These are factors that generally increase rates of maternal death and maternal complications ... This has also been the experience of Texans." In a statement to Houston Public Media, a DSHS spokesperson said the report "isn't delayed," and that DSHS and the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Review Committee (MMMRC) were working to "strengthen the report." "The acting commissioner has asked the committee to strengthen the report by further describing its work around preventability, better defining the sources of its recommendations, and making clear connections between the underlying data, findings, and recommendations," the spokesperson said. The spokesperson also said a new provision to the Texas Health and Safety Code — passed by the state legislature in June 2025 as part of HB 4666 — now allows reports to be submitted no later than Dec. 1. Speaking to Texas Public Radio's David Martin Davies on Texas Matters, White said the new release date could also pose issues for state lawmakers, who are scheduled to meet for a legislative session starting in January. "With a delay in the report, there is not going to be an opportunity for people who are seeking office to be able to propose what their solutions would be to address maternal deaths in the state," White said. "There isn't going to be a lot of time for lawmakers to examine the report, interpret its findings, and start to identify solutions that they want to propose." White said another issue with the forthcoming report is that it omitted deaths from 2022 and 2023 due to the COVID pandemic. "It is problematic that the deaths from 2022 and 2023 are being omitted because these were the first two years that Texas' full abortion ban was in effect," White said. "We know from other reports that there are pregnant Texans who have been unable to get the evidence-based care that they need to address pregnancy complications, and we know at least some of those Texans have died as a result." In the same week that DSHS announced it would not release the report until December, ProPublica published a comprehensive report showing ectopic pregnancy deaths in the U.S. nearly doubled over the past several years. According to ProPublica, states with abortion bans saw the largest increases — including Texas, despite the state's abortion ban having an exception for ectopic pregnancies. According to the Mayo Clinic, an ectopic pregnancy typically occurs in the first trimester and is the result of a pregnancy developing outside the uterus, causing severe bleeding that can result in death if not treated. An ectopic pregnancy cannot proceed normally, and the fertilized egg cannot survive. When it comes to the importance of collecting data on maternal mortality, Fletcher said it’s important to remember that each statistic represents a person. "People that are affected by adverse pregnancy outcomes or families that have lost loved ones from maternal death, they deserve answers," Fletcher said. "They deserve the data to understand that's happening, and they also deserve to know that people are working to improve maternal care across the state." Texas Public Radio's David Martin Davies contributed to this report. title: It's 2026, And I'm Playing GTA V For The First Time - aftermath.site
content: Without any nostalgia or youthful memories, Grand Theft Auto V is a strange game to experience I’ve been broadly immune from the GTA VI hype, not for any principled reasons but because I’ve just never played a Grand Theft Auto game. This has been largely circumstantial, as someone who didn’t own a console when they all released and who tends to dislike driving games. But the recent flurry of GTA VI looks got curiosity gnawing at my brain, wanting to share in the excitement of my peers and feeling drawn to a big open world to explore. And since VI won’t be coming to PC until god-knows-when, I’ve decided to do the only thing I can: finally install the copy of GTA V that’s been sitting on my computer for years. I picked up GTA V when it was free on the Epic store all the way back in 2020, my curiosity largely piqued by having spent years editing Zack Zwiezen’s stories about GTA Online for Kotaku. Zack made the game sound like a weird alternate universe full of the kind of day-to-day life management that I love about survival games, and I hoped the single-player would be that but without other players griefing me into quitting. “I could be a GTA guy,” I confidently told myself in 2020, before proceeding to never think about the game sitting in my Epic library again. A few weekends ago I finally decided to install it. This took a while: Between the Epic store being, well, itself, and my Rockstar account deciding I didn’t exist over and over until it randomly decided oh no wait I did, between account syncs that warned me they failed but didn’t seem to affect anything to having to install BattleEye, my first hour with the game was just a maze of pop-ups and error messages. Once I got into the game, though, things have run pretty smoothly. (Well, smoothly barring that it seems like the combination of using Epic and installing the game on a new SSD means that I can’t tell if my screenshots aren’t saving at all, or if they’re just being saved to some place where I have no hope of finding them. So sorry for the lack of images in this post; I didn’t realize until it was too late! Rest assured every screenshot I took was terrible anyway.) It’s weird to play a very old GTA when I’ve never played one before, and when my only reference for this style of Rockstar game is having not finished Red Dead Redemption 2. I’ve struggled a bit with the tutorials, which appear as tiny text prompts in the upper left of my screen and frequently disappear before I can internalize them. In Franklin’s first “real” mission, where he has to shoot a man fleeing on a motorbike while driving, I kept missing or misunderstanding which buttons I had to press so many times that I had to pause the game and go Google it. I then proceeded to fail the execution of this mechanic so many times that the game finally let me skip the mission, a choice I have continued to make every time the mechanic has arisen, and which I’m sure will have no consequences on my time with the rest of the game at all. Mostly what I’ve done in the game so far is wander around. I’ve only done a couple of Franklin’s missions and two of Michael’s, spending the rest of my time switching between the characters to explore their various neighborhoods. The world is definitely big–the other night I thought I was driving Michael toward one of his question mark sidequests, but when I couldn’t find it I instead walked the whole beach to the fairgrounds, rode the rides, then stole a jet ski and tried to see if I could circumnavigate the entirety of the map. Things hit a snag when I stopped to explore a little island and returned to find my jet ski had not just floated away but seemingly despawned. I stole a boat and kept going, before irrevocably beaching the boat and ending up having to walk for ages through rural dirt roads until I could find a car. A lot of my in-game time has been spent this way: stranding myself on the farthest edges of the map and having to time-consumingly work my way inland again. I also spent multiple in-game days attempting to locate a bicycle. When I discovered that I couldn’t just buy a bike from the in-game internet and store it in Michael’s garage, I wandered the streets of Los Santos hoping to come across one. Eventually I turned to the real-life internet for help, which told me bikes could be found at the beach, the only place in GTA V I can reliably navigate myself to. But I spent full nights and days skulking around parking lot bike racks hoping someone with a bike would come by while they steadfastly did not. Eventually, I walked my way to a bike rental place and nicked one there, which has led to me biking all over town in Michel’s ridiculous jeans and coat, with the current aim of getting back to a national park I passed so I can do some off-road riding. (The game is way more fun on a bike than in a car, if you ask me.) While exploring is what I most like to do in open-world games anyway, it’s also been a way to ease myself into what GTA V actually seems to be. The atmosphere is crass in a way games aren’t anymore–one of the first interactable businesses I came across was a strip club where I could watch a shiny, skimpily-dressed woman writhe in front of me. I also went to a movie, in which a cartoon robot murdered a female robot for rejecting his advances. There are poop and dick and sex and gay jokes everywhere, in a way I think most games, if they haven’t rejected them outright, are at least more artful with today. Maybe some of this was funny in 2013, but in 2026 it mostly feels embarrassing. In his 2022 re-review of the game for Polygon, Cameron Kunzelman wrote that “Back when the game originally released, I called it conservative… Now I would call it out of touch — even for the era in which it was released.” Some of the game feels like it’s trying to have its cake and eat it too, leaning on the South Park defense of making fun of everyone while still essentially being the thing it’s making fun of. There’s a crude cynicism to its humor that, looking through the lens of 2026, is hard to write off as simply dated. And it feels like it’s trying to appeal to a particular vision of “gamers” that isn’t just inaccurate today, but toxic in a different way than it was in 2013. It’s bizarre to play a game whose satirical politics are closer to the Tea Party than MAGA; even though so many of the same conspiracies and hatreds carry through, lines of thought that felt easy to write off or mock back then feel much more serious today. And it’s kind of shocking to play a game that feels like it’s both teasing and catering to a vision of an audience that was crafted before Gamergate. So many of the game’s jokes feel like Gamergate dog whistles, and I have to keep reminding myself that they can’t be, because there weren’t those dogs to whistle at when Rockstar’s developers were making the game. The elements of what would become Gamergate were there, of course; there’s a prescience to GTA V, at the same time as I think there’s no way its developers could have known precisely what they were predicting. I feel weird being disgusted by some of the game, because that reaction veers so close to the moral panics surrounding the GTA series that get wielded against video games as a whole. On the plus side, it also makes the current conservative backlash to GTA VI even more hilarious. GTA looms so large in the public imagination, and is so weight-bearing to the current video game industry, that it’s hard to experience V for the first time just as itself, to not read so much into every billboard and radio spot and activity and character. There’s so much more of it that I need to experience before I can really understand what it is and what it’s doing. But with all the baggage around it, and with what I’ve seen so far when I get too close to the game’s core, I’m not totally sure that I want to. I’ve had more fun just exploring the world, even as I keep brushing against things I think are closed to me until I advance more of the plot. I want to open up all the secrets and mysteries that Zack’s stories made sound so enticing, even as I’m worried what I might find there. GTA V is a strange game to come to without any nostalgia; I’m not quite sure if I’m enjoying it, or what it could look like to enjoy it for the first time in 2026. I would really like to get far enough to buy a better bicycle, though. It's a shooter that asks you an important question: do you want to feel like a badass every 3.5 seconds? Half-Life: Alyx remains the big budget killer app of VR. But playing it again makes you wonder if anyone will ever be allowed to match that ambition. The Trails in the Sky series has always understood that the big heroics aren’t the only thing that make a hero.
